Actual Article Body:
Award-winning journalists and filmmakers Phelim McAleer and Ann McElhinney announced the creation of a $10,000 prize for young citizen journalists who pursue truth and uncover groundbreaking stories.

The married couple, who wrote a play about the horrific October 7 terrorist attacks and produced the film My Son Hunter, among other highly influential investigative works, announced the Shillman Journalism Prize through their organization, the Unreported Story Society. The pair are looking for a story “the mainstream media won’t tell.”

“You don’t need us to tell you something is broken. Every day, too many real stories of real importance are ignored, because they don’t fit the ‘narrative.’ Or the stories are misreported to hide the truth,” the award website reads. “But journalism no longer belongs to legacy newsrooms.”

“The future stories that will shape our country are emerging from new spaces. They come from students, citizens, and independent writers who are hungry for the truth. And are willing to do the work. The Shillman Journalism Prize exists to find these stories … and the people bold enough to tell them,” the announcement continues.

The Shillman Prize, which is funded by a grant from Doctor Bob Shillman and The Shillman Foundation, is open to people under the age of 25 who are not employed full-time as a journalist and are living legally in the U.S.

Contestants may submit original reporting — not an opinion piece — to the prize website. After the submission window closes, an expert panel will select the top ten submissions, and the stories will be published to Substack. Then, the public will vote on the winners.

First prize receives $10,000, followed by $5,000 for second place, and $2,500 for third place.

“We want a story that hasn’t been told, or hasn’t been told properly — the kind of story that is often sitting right on your doorstep, in your town, or in your state,” McAleer wrote in a post to Substack.

“You don’t need to travel to exotic locations. The best stories are frequently the ones closest to home. You can dig up documents under the Freedom of Information Act. Or, more often than not, the key documents are already publicly available — it’s just that mainstream journalists often choose to ignore them because the story doesn’t fit the narrative they want,” he continued. “Or maybe you know someone — a neighbour, a relative, a local official, a whistleblower — who has a story the rest of the country needs to hear. A powerful interview can win this prize.”

“We’re not asking you to put your life on the line. We’re simply asking you to be nosy. To ask awkward questions. To cause a bit of trouble with the truth,” he added. “If you’re under 25 and you think you’ve found the story everyone else missed — or the one the media actively wants covered up — this is your moment.”

The top prize will be announced in spring of 2027. Full contest rules can be read here.

How the tragic distinction of losing the most people on 9/11 brought one World Trade Center firm closer together

Of Cantor Fitzgerald’s 960 New York workers, 658 died, along with 50 contractors and visitors. Another 61 were lost at Euro Brokers, which is now part of Cantor.

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

It’s a distinction no one wants. Cantor Fitzgerald lost more loved ones on 9/11 than any other organization.

The firm’s offices occupied the 101st through 105th floors of the World Trade Center’s North Tower, above where American Airlines Flight 11 struck at 8:46 a.m. Of Cantor’s 960 New York workers, 658 died, along with 50 contractors and visitors. Another 61 were lost at Euro Brokers, which is now part of Cantor.

Every number was a person. Every person had a family. Every family has a story worth remembering. Edie is a Cantor family member. Her office was on the 101st floor, but she wasn’t there that morning. Her brother Gary died on the 104th floor. Her other brother, Howard, then Cantor Fitzgerald’s Chairman and CEO, was spared because he was taking his son to the first day of kindergarten.

On Sept. 14, 2001, Edie and Howard co-founded the Cantor Fitzgerald Relief Fund to help the victims’ relatives rebuild their lives. Many were strangers. They became family.

Caroline joined Cantor Fitzgerald in 2002. At the firm’s annual Charity Day, which raises money for hundreds of charities around the world and disaster relief efforts, she would ask the movie stars, athletes and colleagues who attended: “Where were you on September 11?”

Early replies mirrored her own experiences, as people were headed for work or school drop-off. But with the passing years, the answers changed: high-school chemistry, middle-school homeroom, first grade. Then the inevitable. “I wasn’t born yet,” said a twentysomething actor. Soon, we had memorial volunteers with no firsthand memory of the attacks.

Each September 11, we say “Always remember.” Many post #NeverForget. But the painful truth is that memory fades.

Edie thought back to laying out Cantor’s names with meaningful adjacencies for the National September 11 Memorial. She used to know every name of the lost; 25 years later, those names can be harder to summon. If our own memories were fading, what would a generation or two removed recall?

With the 25th anniversary approaching, we decided the voices of Cantor’s families needed to speak directly to the next generations.

To preserve these memories, Cantor families submitted 176 essays, letters, poems and recollections for “The Families: 9/11 Anthology of Love, Loss and Lessons of Resilience.” We were profoundly changed by their determination and hope.

Burn survivors write of gratitude. A West Point cadet who lost his brother channels his grief into a PTSD program for veterans. A father embraces deep faith after losing two sons. Mothers describe raising children with joy against impossible odds.

And we heard from people who weren’t yet born, like the son who never met his father and now finds a path forward even as he grapples with generational grief.

Others write candidly about addiction and turning pain into purpose through service and philanthropy.

We know first-hand that revisiting the heartbreak of Sept. 11 is not easy. In working on the anthology, Edie recalled 20-hour days writing thousands of checks by hand to widows and new mothers, building support groups and family networks from nothing and attending too many funerals. Returning to her last call with Gary is always painful.

The true gift of “The Families” is in the lessons its contributors share: how to show up for each other, find a mission bigger than your own pain, and allow joy and grief to share a sentence. Those lessons belong to anyone who has had to keep living after losing someone.Edith Lutnick is Co-Founder, president and executive director of the Cantor Fitzgerald Relief Fund. Caroline Aiken Koster is general counsel of the Cantor Fitzgerald Relief Fund and a senior Cantor Fitzgerald corporate lawyer. “The Families: 9/11 Anthology of Love, Loss and Lessons of Resilience” is out now and all proceeds from the book benefit the Cantor Fitzgerald Relief Fund.

New York is getting the backseat treatment at the GOP midterm convention this week, with its delegation being shoved in the left rear corner of the arena in a significant downgrade from the 2016 and 2024 party gatherings.

Actual Article Body:

DALLAS — New York is getting the backseat treatment at the GOP midterm convention this week, with its delegation being placed in the left rear corner of the arena, marking a significant downgrade from the 2016 and 2024 party gatherings.

In the past, despite being a Democratic stronghold, New York seemingly benefited from being President Trump’s native state and nabbed prestigious convention seating. But this go-around, the Trump connection isn’t delivering that.

Some New York Republicans in Dallas were surprised to hear of the rear seating, but tried to take the decision in stride.

“Seating doesn’t matter,” David Laska, the communications director of the New York state GOP, told The Post. “We are honored that Rep. Mike Lawler and one of our House candidates, Mike LiPetri, will be featured speakers.

“More importantly, we are working hand-in-hand with the RNC and other national Republican organizations to make sure we keep our House majority and fire Kathy Hochul in November.”

A Republican National Committee official told The Post that the downgrade this year was by no means meant to be a dig at New York — or any other state. The official noted this is the first time the GOP has done a midterm convention, and the seating was a “game of Tetris” based on how many attendees each state sent.

Unlike presidential conventions with a fixed number of delegates per state who have official functions like voting, the midterm convention attendees have no electoral duties and have paid, in some cases, thousands of dollars to state parties for a crack at the honorary delegate seat.

“It’s a giant puzzle based off of how many people each state has and how they fit on the floor,” the official said of seating choices. “This is not a slight by any means.”

Florida, home to Trump’s official residence in Mar-a-Lago, retained good seating in the front left side of the arena at the 20,000-seat American Airlines Center, home to the NBA’s Mavericks and NHL’s Stars.

However, the seats closest to the stage are not designated to a state, but reserved for “Front Row Joes”  – which is the nickname Trump has dubbed for his biggest fans who follow him around the country to attend his events.

Back in 2024, New York’s delegation earned prime front-row seating, just to the side of the main stage, while Florida enjoyed the center, front-row spot.

In 2016, the Empire State had the highly coveted center front-row spot, with Florida just behind it. The 2020 convention was complicated by the COVID-19 pandemic.

Typically, state delegation seating at party conventions is a show of how influential they are. Oftentimes, battleground states and states where presidential or vice presidential nominees were born get coveted positions.

This week’s so-called “Trump-a-palooza” midterm convention is unprecedented for the GOP. Traditionally,  Republicans and Democrats hold their national party conventions in presidential cycles, when they have to officially coronate their standard-bearer and choose the party platform.

Republicans won’t be doing either of those tasks at the convention confab this week. But at the president’s request, the GOP’s Trump-a-palooza event will mirror key aspects of national party conventions in presidential cycles.

That includes the tradition of state delegates sitting together for the speeches on the arena floor.

Tickets for Michigan’s delegation clocked in at $7,500 for an individual and $10,000 for a couple to become an honorary delegate. Texas’s price tag for being an honorary delegate clocked in at $20,000, the HuffPost reported.

The event is doubling as a mega fundraiser for Republicans and a political stimulant intended to dramatically energize the voting base, 55 days out from the Nov. 3 midterm election.

Connecticut towns are installing license plate reading cameras on school buses

In New Haven, which installed the technology on more than 300 buses earlier this year, cameras have already recorded 12,000 incidents.

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

City and town leaders across Connecticut have been fielding growing pushback from residents over automated license plate readers, which opponents say raise a range of concerns about privacy.

But as many state and local leaders have called for a pause on the technology to weigh new policy guidance, several towns are installing AI-powered license plate readers on school buses.

More than half a dozen towns — including Vernon, Bridgeport, Danbury, Shelton, Stratford, North Haven and New Haven — have contracted with a company called BusPatrol, which installs the technology on the towns’ bus fleets, then uses it to gather footage of any motorist passing a bus that’s displaying flashing red signal lights.

The company’s technicians log the events and provide the recordings to local law enforcement.

Unlike some license plate reading cameras — such as those owned and operated by the company Flock Safety — BusPatrol’s aren’t continuously monitoring the roads.

They are triggered “only when a school bus is stopped with its warning lights and stop arm engaged,” a spokesperson from BusPatrol said.

Since 2011, Connecticut has allowed digital video as evidence of a violation.

A 2024 law change put more power in the hands of municipalities to establish video monitoring systems and issue fines.

And so far, they have caught quite a few.

In New Haven, which installed the technology on more than 300 buses earlier this year, cameras have already recorded 12,000 incidents.

Marc Petruzzi, chief of police in Vernon — which announced its rollout last month — said the town installed the cameras to avoid future tragedies.

“Passing a stopped school bus is one of the most dangerous things that a driver can do,” he said at a press conference announcing the initiative.

In the first three days of the program, BusPatrol cameras caught almost 100 motorists passing school buses, said David Owens, a spokesman for the town.

Authorities announced a major breakthrough in a decades-old cold case, identifying human remains found nearly 49 years ago in North Carolina as belonging to a runaway 15-year-old girl who disappeared from Maryland.

Authorities said the manner of death remained undetermined, but the case was being investigated as a homicide. They said the remains were found in a wooded area near a Wilson County manufacturing facility roughly five hours south of Blizzard’s home.

A medical examiner determined the remains had likely been there for six months to two years and belonged to a white female between 16 and 23 years old.

In the decades that followed, the case went cold as forensic technology was not advanced enough to identify the remains, authorities said.

“For years, investigators compared dental records against missing persons cases without finding a match,” the SBI said.

When the case qualified for advanced DNA testing, forensic scientists extracted preserved genetic material from a bone sample, according to the authorities.

“A genealogy service used the profile to trace potential relatives, pointing investigators toward a 15-year-old girl who had run away from Monkton, Maryland, in the spring of 1977,” the SBI said.

The identification was made with assistance from the FBI’s NCIC Investigation and Operational Assistance Group, the Maryland Department of State Police Homicide Unit and the Raleigh Police Department’s Intel Unit, authorities said.

That's because U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani has blocked USPS from refusing to deliver ballots to voters in states where election officials do not turn over voter lists to the mailing agency and do not have certain specific barcodes on their ballot envelopes.

Judges may face unprecedented decisions this election. A new guide seeks to help

The idea of law enforcement taking possession of ballots in the middle of an active election used to be considered impossible. Now, it's a scenario voting officials — and judges — are training for.

Actual Article Body:
Miles Parks

In this file photo from 2024, Pennsylvania poll workers demonstrate how ballots are are received, processed, scanned, and securely stored.
                
                    
                    Matthew Hatcher/Getty Images

Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly.

The idea of federal law enforcement seizing ballots in the middle of an active election would have once been considered impossible.

Now, as President Trump continues his unprecedented hunt for voter fraud, ballot seizures and search warrants are scenarios voting officials and the legal community are actively preparing for.

One state election official, who did not have permission to speak publicly, told NPR their office has led three separate statewide trainings this year to prepare for the possibility of law enforcement seeking to take possession of ballots or election materials while the election is ongoing.

And UCLA's Safeguarding Democracy Project released a guide Wednesday, shared first with NPR, to help judges navigate search warrant affidavits related to the voting process.

"Lots of things that were off the table are now on the table," said Rick Hasen, the director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project, and the guide's lead author.

Trump has said he regrets not pushing harder for the federal government to seize election equipment after the 2020 election. Already this year, two different search warrants, executed in Fulton County, Ga., and Riverside County, Calif., involved the seizure of ballots.

All that has voting officials preparing for different worst case scenarios this fall.

"This is the thing we really fear," the state voting official, whose state has conducted the trainings, said in a previous interview with NPR. "[Say] we have really close races [in our competitive districts] then the DOJ, FBI come knocking on one of our county doors and they say, 'We believe there's hijinks going on, we're going to confiscate all the ballots so we can count them.'"

If a warrant were served and ballots were seized before an election is certified, it's possible voting officials wouldn't be able to confidently know how many ballots were returned, or whether the ones that were seized were tampered with.

In elections, this is known as breaking the chain of custody.

"They could do so much damage if they did that," the official said.

Legal experts say it is still an extreme and unlikely scenario. Notably because there is a last line of defense that must sign off on any attempt to seize ballots: a judge.

"Right now, the judiciary writ large has their antennae up, anticipating what might be coming down the pike," said retired federal judge Philip Pro, who served as the chief judge for the District of Nevada. "They're going to be prepared."

The warrant executed at the elections office in Fulton County, Ga., was a wake-up call for the legal community not solely because it happened, but because how it was approved.

"Eventually we got to see the search warrant and it confirmed some of our worst fears," said Hasen. "It contained information about potential fraud in Georgia that was based on discredited conspiracy theories."

Magistrate judges, who are generally the ones dealing with warrant affidavits, are not experts in elections, Hasen said, which means this fall, they could also find themselves wading through dubious claims at a time when misinformation is rampant.

Therefore, one of the UCLA guide's recommendations to judges is not to go it alone.

"One of our key recommendations is to bring election administrators into the conversation," Hasen said.

The process for requesting and granting warrants typically happens in secret, without public hearing or testimony, which limits the court's ability to scrutinize requests, said retired Judge Maureen O'Connor, who served as Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Ohio. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has rejected the chief rabbi's warning that British Jews are at greater risk after the UK announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Miliband said that as a "proud British Jew" he disagreed with UK Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis who described the move as a "truly dark day" that would "succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target".

"We all need to do more to tackle antisemitism," Miliband said, "But I believe we can do that and stand up for British values."

The sanctions on trade with illegal settlements in the West Bank come against a backdrop of rising antisemitic incidents across the UK.

The Community Security Trust (CST), an organisation that provides security support to the Jewish community, recorded 1,926 incidents of anti-Jewish hate across the UK in the first six months of 2026, a 21% increase on the same period in 2025.

The Palestinian presidency welcomed the UK's decision, saying it was "an important step towards confronting Israel's colonial system and its violations against the Palestinian people".

But there has been mixed reaction within the UK Jewish community on the sanctions and possible implications for security.

The chief rabbi called the government's announcement "little more than political flag bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric".

Sir Ephraim said: "Gesture politics of this kind feeds into an increasingly hostile discourse about Israel, and the cumulative effect of such punitive policies is to further embolden those, at home and abroad, who use hatred as a weapon against Jews."

Questioned on Mirvis's comments, Miliband said: "I don't agree with the chief rabbi, someone whom I have great respect."

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme he said "anyone who holds British Jews - or indeed Jews around the world - responsible for the actions of the Israeli government, is engaging in antisemitism, pure and simple."

While, the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) warned the sanctions move "risks becoming a de facto boycott of Israel" and accused Miliband of "yielding to pressure from the most extreme elements of British society".

Germany's chancellor clashes with AfD leader Alice Weidel, saying her migration policy amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.

Actual Article Body:
Merz and Weidel faced off for the first time since Sunday's AfD election victory

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration policy that amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.

Merz was addressing the Bundestag in the aftermath of the anti-immigration party's sweeping victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt where it won almost 44% of the vote, while the chancellor's conservatives saw their vote halved.

Weidel told MPs that voters had shown that Merz's coalition with the centre left was a total failure and his time was up.

Merz hit back saying the AfD had harmed German interests by backing Russia, and its "remigration" policy would affect millions.

It is not yet clear whether the party will be able to form a government or not in Saxony-Anhalt, having fallen three seats short of an outright majority. No far-right party has won power in any of Germany's 16 states since World War Two, and Merz has admitted the "seismic" result has changed Germany.

The AfD's success has been praised by US President Donald Trump, who said "the Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night", linking the victory to "absolutely horrible immigration rules and regulations".

The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been labelled as "right-wing extremist" by German domestic intelligence and the party has promised a "deportation and remigration" offensive targeting irregular migrants.

Repeatedly heckled by AfD MPs, the chancellor told Weidel that one in six skilled workers had a migration background, and if her party had its way then its policy would amount to "nothing other than an ethnic cleansing in the skilled trades based on skin colour and origin".

While the government understood some deportations were needed, he said it made a careful distinction between those who contributed to German prosperity and those without permanent residency.

Disruption by AfD MPs became so loud that at one point Bundestag President Julia KlÃ¶ckner threatened to start expelling people from the chamber: "We are not on a football pitch."

Weidel said mass migration had left Germans with daily knife violence and attacks on trains and in stations, but Merz warned that the AfD's plans would mean that no single care home, hospital or restaurant could function.

As leader of the main opposition party in the Bundestag, Weidel opened the session by telling Merz his Christian Democrats had been "pulverised" in Saxony-Anhalt, after winning 17.2% of the vote, and she accused his government with the Social Democrats of driving Germany towards bankruptcy.

Merz said her party had not won an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt and it would not achieve one in Germany.

"You are and will remain a destructive force," he said, accusing the party of cheating the voters by saying before the election that their candidate for premier, Ulrich Siegmund, would only rule if he won a majority, but hours after the vote deciding to go and find one.

The AfD has opened the door to working with another party, perhaps the left-wing populist BSW, as long as it backs Siegmund to be state premier.

Siegmund's number two in Saxony-Anhalt, has even suggested that Merz's CDU could work with his party, if it abandons the so-called firewall (Brandmauer), under which no mainstream party will work with the far right.

Topic:Veterans

The SA branch of the Headstone Project worries that federal funding does not match a promise made in 2022. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

The South Australian branch of the Headstone Project fears the available funding is much lower than promised pre-election in 2022.

The Headstone Project gives plaques to Australian soldiers who served in World War I, which volunteers say costs about $1,500 per grave.

The federal government did not provide an on-the-record response to questions, but the ABC understands that all eligible applicants have so far been awarded grants.

An organisation that helps to locate and name veterans in unmarked graves in South Australia is raising concerns about whether promised federal funding will be delivered.

The Headstone Project locates World War I veterans in unmarked graves and places a military service headstone there to recognise their service to Australia.

President of the SA branch, John Brownlie, said giving a veteran a headstone cost about $1,500 and that federal government grants contributed $620 toward that cost.

Getting a headstone for this veteran's grave will cost about $1,500. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Before the 2022 federal election, Labor committed $3.7 million in funding for the Headstone Project nationally.

Federal budget papers show $1.4 million over five years from 2025-2026 has been allocated for a range of memorial initiatives, including the Marking (First World War) Private Graves Grants program, which is the grant the Headstone Project applies for.

Those grant guidelines, as seen by the ABC, show only $58,000 is available nationally for this financial year.

The Headstone Project SA believes that number to be below what should be available.

These two nurses were given headstones that recognised their service. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Mr Brownlie queried the amount.

"Look at what you've [the federal government] promised, and look at what you've delivered, because there's a vast discrepancy," Mr Brownlie said.

"I think the behaviour of the government, quite frankly, is egregious."

The federal government did not provide an on-the-record response to the concerns raised by the Headstone Project SA, but the ABC understands all eligible applications have been awarded grant funding.

Ian Hopley is a former police officer who now investigates unmarked graves to provide military headstones. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Ian Hopley is a retired police officer who now assists with finding graves, determining that a veteran is buried in the grave and then researching and contacting living relatives.

The team searches cemetery records and picks out males of enlistment age born between 1870 and 1900; they then cross-check that with the national archives and find the graves of forgotten veterans.

Mr Hopley said the SA branch had provided headstones to nearly 200 servicemen and women and that about 500 were known around the state still to be waiting.

"Our work will go on for a very long time, provided we get the right funding and support," he said.

Mr Hopley said he came from a military family and believed the people in unmarked graves should be recognised for their service.
